prompt: For a positive Fenwick index, `i & -i` isolates its lowest set bit. What does that tell you about entry `t[i]`?

options.text: It tells you the number of non-zero values in the whole array.
options.explanation: The operation depends only on the index, not the stored values.

options.text: It gives the length of the stored block ending at that index.
options.explanation: Correct. That block length determines how a query skips to the preceding block.

options.text: It identifies the highest occupied index in the tree.
options.explanation: The lowest set bit is local to this index.

options.text: It gives the sum already stored in the entry.
options.explanation: Index arithmetic determines coverage, not the data-dependent sum.

workedExample: A Fenwick entry covers a backward-looking block. The lowest set bit supplies that block’s length. Subtracting the length moves a query to the end of the preceding uncovered block; the bit trick is useful because it identifies coverage without a separate pointer.

prompt: In a Fenwick tree, which elements does `t[6]` hold the sum of?

options.explanation: Only indices that are powers of two hold whole prefixes. 6 is not a power of two.
Single elements are held at odd indices, whose lowest set bit is 1. 6 is even.
Correct. 6 is `110`, its lowest set bit is 2, so `t[6]` covers the 2 elements ending at 6: `a[5]` and `a[6]`.
Blocks end at i and extend *backwards*; `t[i]` never includes elements after i.

workedExample: Index six has lowest set bit two. Its block ends at six and contains two elements, so it covers positions five and six. Blocks never extend to the right of their entry’s index. A whole prefix is stored directly only at a power-of-two index.
